title: Why I Left Software for Soil
author: Shubham Saurabh
excerpt: A B.Tech CSE graduate's journey from desktop computing to sustainable farming in Nalanda, Bihar.
content:
I still remember the day I sat in front of my laptop in Bengaluru, debugging a Kubernetes cluster for a fintech startup, and thought: 'What am I actually building?'

Don't get me wrong — software engineering is beautiful. The logic, the architecture, the satisfaction of a clean deploy. My B.Tech in Computer Science gave me a lens to see the world as systems: inputs, processes, outputs. But somewhere between the sprints and standups, I felt the output missing.

### The Return

I came back to Mahamadpur — my ancestral village in Nalanda, Bihar — in early 2024. Not as a tourist, but to stay. The first thing I noticed: the soil. Dark, alluvial, Gangetic soil that has fed civilizations for millennia. And yet, the farmers around me were struggling. Input costs were high. Market prices were opaque. Traditional knowledge was eroding.

I saw a system begging to be optimized.

### The Intersection

That's when JeeVan was born. Not as a 'startup idea' but as a necessity. I started with a simple observation: farmers need what engineers build — real-time data, accessible platforms, and efficient systems. The plant nursery came first. Saplings, seeds, and composting kits. Then the tech consulting — helping other small businesses go digital. Then the creative studio, because storytelling is how we connect.

### What I've Learned

Soil doesn't care about your GitHub profile. A plant doesn't care about your tech stack. But when you apply systems thinking to agriculture — tracking soil health, optimizing water use, connecting farmers directly to buyers — magic happens. The same rigor that debugs a race condition can debug a pest infestation.

JeeVan today is a living proof that technology and agriculture aren't opposites. They're the same thing, viewed from different angles. And from this small village in Bihar, we're proving it one sapling at a time.

title: What Grows in Nalanda — A Seasonal Guide
author: Shubham Saurabh
excerpt: Month-by-month planting guide for Bihar's climate. Heirloom varieties that thrive in the Gangetic plain.
content:
Nalanda district sits in the heart of the Indo-Gangetic plain — one of the most fertile regions on Earth. With deep alluvial soil, abundant groundwater, and a subtropical climate, this land can grow almost anything. The question isn't 'what grows here?' but 'what should you plant when?'

### Rabi Season (October–March)

This is our main growing season. Winters are mild (8–20°C), perfect for:

- **Wheat (HD-2967, PBW-343):** Our staple. Plant in November, harvest in March-April. The Gangetic soil produces some of India's best wheat.
- **Mustard (Pusa Bold):** Yellow fields in February. Cold-pressed mustard oil from Nalanda is legendary.
- **Chickpea, Lentil, Pea:** Pulses thrive in our winter. Zero chemical input needed.
- **Coriander, Fenugreek:** Leafy greens through December-February.

### Kharif Season (June–September)

Monsoon planting. Our rainfall averages 1000mm, concentrated in these months:

- **Rice (Katarani, traditional Magahi variety):** The pride of Bihar. Plant in July, harvest in October-November.
- **Maize, Sorghum:** Rain-fed cereals for both grain and fodder.
- **Turmeric, Ginger:** High-value rhizomes. Our turmeric rivals Salem varieties.
- **Moringa:** Plant once, harvest for 20 years. The drumstick tree is a superfood factory.

### Zaid Season (March–June)

The summer gap. Hot (35–45°C) but manageable with irrigation:

- **Cucumber, Bottle Gourd, Bitter Gourd:** Fast-growing summer vegetables.
- **Watermelon, Muskmelon:** Sandy-loam patches near the riverbeds.
- **Green Manure (Sesbania):** Grow it, plow it in. Free nitrogen.

### Heirloom Stars

These aren't in any government seed catalog. They're passed down through families:

- **Magahi Paan:** The betel leaf that gave Magadh its reputation. Grown under shade nets.
- **Desi Katarani Rice:** Short-grain, aromatic. Grown by maybe 50 families now.
- **Makhana (Foxnut):** Technically an aquatic crop. The ponds of northern Bihar produce 90% of the world's makhana.

### My Advice

Start with 3 crops. One staple, one cash crop, one vegetable. Don't chase trends. Build soil health first — the crops will follow.

title: Natural vs Chemical — JeeVan's Philosophy
author: Shubham Saurabh
excerpt: Why we choose natural farming methods. The science behind soil health and the economics of organic produce.
content:
Let me be clear: I'm not anti-science. I'm a computer scientist. I believe in data, evidence, and reproducible results. And the data on natural farming is compelling.

### The Soil is Alive

A teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are humans on Earth. Fungi, bacteria, protozoa, nematodes — a subterranean metropolis that chemical fertilizers systematically destroy. Urea doesn't feed plants; it bypasses the soil food web. Over time, soil becomes inert, addicted to synthetic inputs.

Natural farming restores this web. Jeevamrut (fermented cow dung, urine, jaggery, and pulse flour) feeds the microbes, which in turn feed the plants. It's slower than a urea top-dress, but the results compound.

### The Economics

A Bihari farmer growing wheat with chemicals spends roughly ₹8,000–10,000 per acre on inputs (urea, DAP, pesticides). Natural farming cuts this to ₹1,500–2,000 — mostly for labor and cow-based preparations. The yield might dip 10-15% in year one. By year three, it matches or exceeds chemical yields because the soil is actually alive.

Farmers in Andhra Pradesh's Community Managed Natural Farming program report 30% higher net incomes after 3 years. Not because of higher yields, but because of lower costs.

### Nutrition Density

This is the silent crisis. Chemical-grown vegetables are bigger, shinier, and nutritionally hollow. Brix meters (measuring sugar/mineral content) consistently show natural-grown produce at 8-12 brix versus 3-5 for chemical. That tomato might look perfect, but it's mostly water.

### Our Approach at JeeVan

We're not purists. We use:
- **Natural fertilizers:** Jeevamrut, vermicompost, green manure
- **Biopesticides:** Neem oil, dashparni ark, brahmastra
- **No-till where possible:** Preserves soil structure
- **Mulching:** Retains moisture, suppresses weeds

We do use drip irrigation and soil sensors — technology, not chemicals. The goal isn't to reject modernity. It's to use it intelligently.

title: Magahi Heirloom Varieties — Bihar's Agricultural Heritage
author: Shubham Saurabh
excerpt: Magahi Paan, Katarani Rice, Desi Makhana — the indigenous crops that define Bihar's food culture.
content:
Magadh — the ancient kingdom that gave us the Mauryan Empire, Buddhism, and the world's first university at Nalanda. For 2,500 years, this land has also given us something equally profound: agricultural biodiversity.

### Magahi Paan (Betel Leaf)

If you've ever had a truly great paan, chances are the leaf came from Magadh. Magahi paan is different — smaller, more aromatic, with a distinct sweetness that lingers. It's grown under shade nets (called 'bareja') that create a microclimate of humidity and filtered light. A single well-maintained bareja can produce paan for 25 years.

The problem: commercial paan varieties from Bengal and Odisha are flooding the market. They're bigger, cheaper, and lack the Magahi character. We're working with 12 local growers to preserve and propagate authentic Magahi paan genetics.

### Katarani Rice

'Katarni' means 'scissors' in Hindi, possibly referring to the pointed grain shape. This short-grain aromatic rice was once the pride of Bhagalpur and Nalanda. It has a natural popcorn-like fragrance when cooked. Unlike Basmati (long-grain, elongates when cooked), Katarani is sticky and aromatic — perfect for kheer, pulao, and everyday meals.

Today, less than 100 acres grow Katarani across the entire district. Hybrid varieties and BPT rice have displaced it. We've collected seeds from 6 aging farmers and are multiplying them in our nursery. Our goal: 500 acres of Katarani in Nalanda by 2030.

### Desi Makhana (Foxnut)

Bihar produces 90% of the world's makhana, primarily from the ponds of Darbhanga, Madhubani, and northern Nalanda. Makhana is an aquatic crop — the seeds of Euryale ferox, a water lily. Harvesting is brutal work: farmers wade chest-deep in ponds, collect the seeds, roast them, and pop them.

The tragedy: most makhana farmers are the poorest in the value chain. A kilogram of raw makhana sells for ₹300-400. Roasted and packaged? ₹1,200. Flavored and branded? ₹2,000+. We're working to connect makhana farmers directly to consumers through our platform.

### Other Heirloom Treasures

- **Marcha Rice:** A red rice variety from Banka, iron-rich, traditionally given to new mothers.
- **Desi Arhar (Pigeon Pea):** Smaller than commercial varieties but twice the flavor. Perfect for sattu.
- **Kaala Jeera (Black Cumin):** Not the Kashmiri variety. A local spice that grows wild in the Kharif season.

### Why This Matters

Every time a farmer switches to a hybrid variety for 10% higher yield, we lose genetic diversity we can never recover. These heirloom varieties have survived droughts, floods, and pests for centuries. They carry adaptations that no laboratory can engineer. Preserving them isn't nostalgia — it's insurance for our food future.

title: Zero Budget Natural Farming — A Practical Guide
author: Shubham Saurabh
excerpt: How to farm without spending on external inputs. Jeevamrut, Bijamrit, mulching, and crop rotation.
content:
Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF) was popularized by Padma Shri Subhash Palekar, but the principles are ancient. The core idea: you don't need to buy anything from outside your farm. Everything the soil needs is already there.

### The Four Pillars

**1. Jeevamrut — The Microbial Inoculant**

Mix in 200 liters of water:
- 10 kg fresh cow dung (desi breed preferred)
- 5-10 liters cow urine
- 2 kg jaggery (or sugarcane juice)
- 2 kg pulse flour (besan, any dal flour)
- Handful of soil from under a big tree

Ferment for 48-72 hours in shade, stirring twice daily. Apply within 7 days. This one preparation replaces urea, DAP, and potash — not by adding NPK directly, but by activating the soil biology that makes NPK available to plants.

**2. Bijamrit — Seed Treatment**

Same ingredients as Jeevamrut but in smaller quantities (for 10 liters): 500g dung, 500ml urine, 50g lime, 50g soil. Soak seeds for 30 minutes before sowing. This protects against seed-borne diseases and jumpstarts germination.

**3. Achhadan — Mulching**

Keep the soil covered at all times. Crop residue, dry leaves, straw — anything organic. Benefits:
- Retains moisture (30-50% less irrigation)
- Suppresses weeds
- Moderates soil temperature
- Feeds earthworms and microbes as it decomposes

**4. Waaphasa — Soil Aeration**

Don't over-till. Don't compact the soil with heavy machinery. Maintain 30-40% air in the soil. Earthworms do the tilling for you.

### Pest Management — Natural Arsenal

- **Neemastra:** 5 kg neem leaves crushed in 100L water + cow urine. Ferment 24 hours. Spray for sucking pests.
- **Brahmastra:** Neem + Datura + Custard Apple leaves. Nuclear option for severe infestations.
- **Dashparni Ark:** 10 different bitter leaves fermented in cow urine. Broad-spectrum, preventative.

### Crop Rotation That Works

For Bihar conditions, try this 3-year rotation:

Year 1: Legume (pigeon pea, chickpea) → fixes nitrogen
Year 2: Cereal (wheat, rice) → uses the nitrogen
Year 3: Vegetable/Leafy → shallow roots, different nutrient profile

Then repeat. Add 2 border rows of marigold or sunflower — they attract pollinators and trap pests.

### The Real Secret

ZBNF isn't a set of recipes. It's a mindset shift. You're not feeding plants. You're feeding soil. The plants will feed themselves. It takes 2-3 years for soil to fully recover from chemical dependency. Be patient. The first year is the hardest. But the second year you'll notice fewer pests, darker soil, and better taste. By year three, you'll wonder why anyone farms any other way.

At JeeVan, we practice ZBNF on 80% of our farm. The other 20% is experimental — testing new heirloom varieties and soil amendments. But the lesson is consistent: work with nature, not against it, and she rewards you abundantly.
